nameStory: This microscopic green alga gets its scientific name from the Latin 'lacuna' meaning 'gap' or 'hollow space,' referring to the characteristic holes or spaces in its delicate net-like structure. The species name 'gracillimum' means 'most slender,' describing its incredibly fine, thread-like appearance under the microscope.
description: Lacunastrum gracillimum is a microscopic freshwater green alga that forms delicate, lace-like colonies in quiet waters. **[Note: This species is extremely rare with only 5 observations in New England - identification details may be uncertain]** These colonies appear as tiny, translucent green films or patches floating just below the water surface or attached to submerged objects. Individual colonies are usually only a few millimeters across, made up of interconnected cells arranged in beautiful geometric patterns that look like nature's own microscopic doilies.

idTips.label: Colony structure
idTips.description: Forms delicate, net-like or lace-like colonies with distinct geometric patterns and small holes throughout the structure

idTips.label: Size and visibility
idTips.description: Colonies are tiny, usually just a few millimeters across, requiring close inspection or magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Color and transparency
idTips.description: Bright green but translucent, creating an almost jewel-like appearance when light passes through

idTips.label: Texture feel
idTips.description: Extremely delicate and fragile - falls apart at the slightest touch, unlike tougher algae mats

idTips.label: Water position
idTips.description: Usually found floating just below the surface or loosely attached to plants and debris in very still water

habitat: Found in quiet, nutrient-rich freshwater environments like small ponds, slow-moving streams, and protected coves of larger lakes throughout New England. Prefers areas with minimal water movement where its delicate colonies won't be disturbed by currents or waves. Often associated with other microscopic algae and aquatic plants in shallow, sun-warmed waters.

seasonality.spring: Colonies begin forming as water temperatures warm and daylight hours increase, often appearing as tiny green specks in quiet waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when colonies are most visible and numerous, especially during warm, calm periods with plenty of sunlight.
seasonality.fall: Colonies may persist into early fall but become less common as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Generally absent from the water column, likely surviving as resistant spores or resting stages in sediments.

funFact: Despite being one of the tiniest organisms you might spot in New England waters, this alga creates some of nature's most intricate geometric art - its colonies form patterns so perfectly symmetrical they look like they were designed by a mathematician!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other microscopic green algae or small bits of green debris floating in water. The key difference is the distinctive net-like pattern with regular holes - most other tiny algae form solid films or irregular clumps rather than lacy, perforated colonies.
contextualKnowledge: **[Uncertain identification details]** This species is extremely rare in New England with very limited observation data. Many microscopic algae require laboratory equipment for definitive identification, so field observations should be considered preliminary unless confirmed by microscopic examination.
compareHints: Since no other Lacunastrum species are documented in New England, compare it with other net-forming green algae in the water column family. Unlike the more common Hydrodictyon (water net), Lacunastrum forms much smaller, more delicate colonies with finer meshwork and is typically found in smaller water bodies rather than larger lakes or rivers.
